body:
Art in the Harappan Civilisation

The Harappan or Indus Civilisation flourished in its mature urban phase from approximately 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE. Its inhabitants developed skilled traditions of stone carving, metal casting, pottery, seal engraving and terracotta modelling. Objects produced for practical use often display considerable artistic refinement.

Harappan art is known mainly through surviving objects rather than written descriptions, because the Indus script has not been deciphered. Sculptures and figurines therefore provide direct evidence of artistic techniques, clothing, ornaments and the representation of human and animal forms. They do not, by themselves, establish the religious or political identity of the people represented.

Stone Sculpture

Stone sculptures from Harappan settlements are relatively few, but several show careful modelling of the human body and facial features. Two important examples are the bearded male bust from Mohenjodaro and a red sandstone male torso associated with Harappa.

The Bearded Male Bust

A famous steatite sculpture from Mohenjodaro represents a bearded man wearing a decorated garment. Steatite is a comparatively soft stone that can be finely carved.

The figure has a neatly trimmed beard, carefully modelled facial features and a shawl passing beneath the right arm and covering the left shoulder. The garment bears a trefoil design, a decorative pattern formed from groups of 3 rounded elements. The half-closed eyes and composed expression contribute to the sculpture's distinctive appearance.

This figure is popularly called the Priest-King. However, that is a conventional modern name, not an established identification. There is no deciphered inscription proving that the person was either a priest or a king.

The Red Sandstone Male Torso

A red sandstone male torso from Harappa demonstrates the sculptor's understanding of bodily proportions. Its shoulders and abdomen are carefully shaped. Socket holes indicate that the head and arms were made separately and attached to the torso.

This example is important because it shows that Harappan sculptors could create three-dimensional human figures using separately prepared components.

Bronze Sculpture

Bronze is an alloy made principally by combining copper with tin. Harappan craftspeople used copper and bronze for objects such as tools, vessels and figurines.

The Dancing Girl of Mohenjodaro

The bronze statuette popularly known as the Dancing Girl was discovered at Mohenjodaro. It is approximately 11 cm tall and is among the best-known examples of Harappan metal sculpture.

The figure portrays a young female standing with one hand resting on her hip. Numerous bangles cover much of her left arm. Her hair is arranged behind her head, and she wears a necklace. The sculpture shows considerable skill in representing human posture and bodily form on a small scale.

The name Dancing Girl describes the appearance traditionally associated with the statuette. It does not establish that the individual was a professional dancer.

The figure was produced by the lost-wax casting technique, in which a model made of wax is used to create a mould for molten metal. The technique allowed artisans to produce shapes that would have been difficult to carve from a solid block of metal.

Animal Sculptures

Harappan metalworkers also produced animal figures, including bulls, buffaloes and other creatures. Their representations emphasise features such as horns, posture and muscular form. These objects demonstrate that metal casting was not restricted to human figures.

The material and findspot of an artefact are often more certain than its traditional name. The Dancing Girl is a bronze figure from Mohenjodaro, while the so-called Priest-King is a steatite sculpture from the same city. Neither conventional name proves the person's occupation or status.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro: Bronze Dancing Girl and steatite bearded male bust.
  • Harappa: Red sandstone male torso with provision for separately attached parts.
  • Dancing Girl: Approximately 11 cm tall; produced by lost-wax casting.
  • Priest-King: Bearded male figure with a trefoil-patterned garment.
  • Trap: The title Priest-King is not proof of priestly or royal authority.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, printed pp. 9–11 and 16–17; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, printed p. 16; National Museum, New Delhi, Museums of India repository, Dancing Girl, accession Hr.5271/195, consulted 17 November 2026.]

body:
Terracotta: Art Made from Fired Clay

Terracotta is clay that has been shaped and hardened by firing. Harappan craftspeople used it to make figurines, toys, small household objects and decorative items.

Clay was comparatively accessible and could be shaped without the specialised equipment needed for metal casting. This made terracotta suitable for producing many different forms, including human figures, animals and movable toys.

Human Figurines

Harappan terracotta figurines include male and female representations. Many female figures have prominent ornaments, elaborate headdresses and deliberately emphasised bodily features.

Some female figurines are traditionally described as Mother Goddess figures. The designation reflects an interpretation that they may have represented a female deity associated with fertility or protection. Their exact meaning is not established. A female terracotta figure should therefore not automatically be treated as proof of goddess worship.

Compared with certain stone and bronze sculptures, many terracotta human figures are more simplified or stylised. Their features may be formed through separately applied pieces of clay, incised lines and prominent decorative elements. The distinction is one of common artistic approaches, not an absolute rule applying to every object.

Animal Figurines and Toys

Terracotta objects include representations of bulls, other animals, birds and wheeled carts. Toy carts, wheels, rattles and whistles are important examples of objects associated with everyday life.

Wheeled terracotta models demonstrate familiarity with wheeled vehicles. They do not, however, reveal every detail of the size, construction or use of actual transport vehicles.

The presence of toys also shows that Harappan craft production served purposes beyond agriculture, trade and formal administration.

Painted Pottery and Decorative Patterns

Harappan pottery was commonly made on the potter's wheel. Red pottery was widespread, and some vessels were decorated with black-painted designs.

The principal distinction is between relatively plain pottery and decorated pottery. Plain vessels were more common, while painted vessels display the craftspeople's ability to organise decorative designs across curved surfaces.

Common Decorative Motifs

  • Geometric designs: Lines, intersecting patterns, circles and other repeated forms.
  • Plant designs: Leaves, branches and related vegetal motifs.
  • Animal and bird designs: Recognisable creatures and simplified natural forms.

Some pottery was covered with a fine slip before painting. A slip is a thin coating of liquid clay applied to the vessel's surface. The painted designs were then incorporated into the finishing and firing process.

Polychrome pottery, decorated using several colours, also occurred but was less common than ordinary red and black-painted pottery.

Beads, Ornaments and Small Decorative Objects

Harappan ornaments were made from several materials, including carnelian, steatite, shell, terracotta, copper, bronze, gold and faience.

Carnelian is a reddish semiprecious stone. It was used to manufacture beads, including finely shaped and drilled examples. Gujarat was an important source of semiprecious stones, and Lothal was a significant centre of bead production.

Bead-making required several skills. Craftspeople shaped the raw material, smoothed and polished the surface, and drilled a hole through which a thread or cord could pass. Some beads received additional decoration.

Faience was an artificially produced material made using substances such as powdered quartz or sand. After shaping and firing, it could acquire a glazed surface. It was used for beads, bangles and small objects.

The finished beads often had carefully controlled shapes, such as spherical, cylindrical or disc-like forms. This shows the connection between decorative craftsmanship and practical knowledge of shape, proportion and measurement.

Distinguishing the Main Craft Traditions

CraftMain materialCharacteristic objects
Stone carvingStone, including steatiteHuman sculptures and carved seals
Metal castingCopper and bronzeHuman and animal figurines
Terracotta modellingFired clayFigurines, toy carts and animals
PotteryClayPlain and painted vessels
Bead-makingSemiprecious stones, shell and faienceOrnaments and decorative beads

Prelims focus

  • Terracotta: Fired clay used for figurines, toys and small objects.
  • Mother Goddess: A traditional interpretation of certain female figurines, not a proven religious identity.
  • Harappan pottery: Predominantly wheel-made; red ware with black designs is characteristic.
  • Carnelian: Reddish semiprecious stone used for beads.
  • Lothal: Important Harappan bead-making centre in Gujarat.
  • Trap: Faience is artificially produced; it is not a naturally occurring gemstone.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, printed pp. 11–15 and 17; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, printed pp. 10–12; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class VI, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, printed pp. 35–37.]

body:
What Is a Harappan Seal?

A seal is an object carrying an engraved design that can be impressed onto a softer material. Harappan seals are among the most characteristic surviving objects of the Indus Civilisation.

Thousands of seals have been discovered at Harappan sites. Many were made from steatite, although seals and related engraved objects were also produced using other materials.

Harappan stamp seals were commonly square, although other shapes are known. A typical example contains an animal figure and a short sequence of signs belonging to the still-undeciphered Indus script.

Animals and Symbols on Seals

The animals represented on Harappan seals include bulls, elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers and other creatures. The figures were often engraved with careful attention to their recognisable features.

A particularly common motif is the so-called unicorn, a single-horned animal represented in profile. The word unicorn is a conventional description of the image. It does not establish that the Harappans possessed or believed in an actual one-horned horse.

Some seals display human figures or more elaborate compositions. The famous seated-figure seal from Mohenjodaro has sometimes been identified as a Pashupati figure. Such religious identifications remain interpretations rather than established readings of the inscription.

Seals were therefore both artistic objects and objects that may have served practical or symbolic purposes.

The Difference Between a Seal and a Sealing

A seal is the engraved stamp. A sealing is the impression left when that stamp is pressed onto a soft material, commonly wet clay.

Seals and sealings were useful in systems involving the storage and movement of goods. A clay sealing could help identify the person or organisation responsible for a package and reveal whether its fastening had been disturbed.

How a Sealed Package Could Work

  1. A bag or package containing goods was closed and tied with a cord.
  2. Wet clay was applied over the knot or fastening.
  3. An engraved seal was pressed into the soft clay, leaving an impression.
  4. The clay dried and formed a marked closure. A recipient could inspect whether it remained intact.

Because the seal was engraved, its impression reproduced the design in reverse relief. Thus, the seal and the resulting sealing were related objects but were not identical.

What Seals Tell Us About Harappan Society

The recurrence of similar seal forms and motifs across widely separated Harappan settlements suggests shared conventions of design and communication.

Seals probably had important roles in trade, the identification of goods and administrative practices. However, the undeciphered inscriptions prevent us from establishing their exact written messages. A suggestion that a seal recorded an owner's name, title or organisation remains a hypothesis rather than a verified translation.

Lothal and Sealings in Gujarat

Lothal, in present-day Gujarat, provides an important connection between Harappan seals and the movement or storage of goods.

Archaeologists discovered numerous clay sealings associated with a structure identified as a warehouse at Lothal. The finds support the interpretation that sealing practices were used in connection with stored commodities and their handling.

The combination of sealings, storage structures and craft production makes Lothal particularly important for understanding how practical systems of identification and exchange may have functioned.

A seal is evidence of an engraved design and, where present, an inscription. A sealing can additionally demonstrate that an impression was made on a particular piece of clay. Neither object automatically reveals the meaning of its script or proves a single specific administrative system.

Prelims focus

  • Usual material: Steatite.
  • Common form: Square stamp seal with an animal motif and a short inscription.
  • Unicorn: A characteristic single-horned animal motif.
  • Sealing: Impression of a seal on a soft material such as clay.
  • Lothal: Clay sealings associated with a warehouse structure.
  • Trap: A seal and a sealing are different objects.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class XII, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, Section 7.1, Seals and Sealings, printed p. 15; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, printed pp. 11–12; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class VI, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, printed pp. 39–40; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal, Tentative List 5918, Description, consulted 17 November 2026.]
